lead: The first Church meets its first quarrel, over food for widows, and solves it by sharing out ministry: the apostles keep to prayer and the word, and seven men full of the Spirit take up the daily service. In the Gospel the disciples cross the lake in the dark and the wind, and Jesus comes to them over the water: “It is I; do not be afraid.” Both scenes show a Church that is never left alone in its difficulties. Psalm 33 asks: “Lord, let your mercy be on us, as we place our trust in you”.

r.h: Seven men full of the Spirit
set: The Jerusalem Church was growing, and with growth came strain. “Hellenists” were Jewish believers who spoke Greek, many of them from Jewish communities outside the land who had settled in Jerusalem. “Hebrews” were Jewish believers whose everyday language was Aramaic. Both groups were Jewish; the difference was language and culture.

Widows without family had no income, and the Jerusalem community cared for them daily. The seven chosen all have Greek names, and one, Nicolaus, was a proselyte, a gentile who had become a Jew. The solution comes from within the group that felt neglected.
str: vv. 2–4: the Twelve propose a solution.
vv. 5–6: the community chooses seven; the apostles pray and lay hands on them.
v. 7: the word spreads, even among the priests.
kw: The key word, used three ways: the daily “distribution” is diakonia (v. 1), “to wait on tables” is diakonein (v. 2), and the apostles’ “serving the word” is diakonia of the word (v. 4). Both are service; neither is lower in God’s eyes.
The word recalls Israel murmuring in the wilderness (Exodus 16). Luke does not hide the Church’s tensions, but shows how the Spirit heals them.
An ancient gesture of blessing and of handing on a task, used for Joshua by Moses (Numbers 27:18–23). In Acts it accompanies prayer and the gift of the Spirit.
vv: It is not right that we should neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables.
Not contempt for practical service, which the seven are chosen to do with the Spirit’s help. It is a question of each one’s calling: the apostles must not be pulled away from the word and prayer.
select from among yourselves seven men of good standing, full of the Spirit and of wisdom,
Even managing food requires the Spirit. The qualities asked for are spiritual before they are practical.
who prayed and laid their hands on them.
The community chooses, but the apostles commission them with prayer and the laying on of hands. The Church has seen in this the pattern of ordination.
a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.
A striking note: many of the temple priests came to faith. The first Church was a Jewish community, and the Gospel took root first among the people of the covenant.
ch: Acts does not call the seven “deacons”, and two of them, Stephen and Philip, are soon seen preaching and baptizing. Yet since St Irenaeus in the second century the Church has seen in this scene the beginning of the diaconate. The Second Vatican Council teaches that deacons receive the laying on of hands “not unto the priesthood, but unto a ministry of service” (Lumen Gentium 29; CCC 1569).

r.h: It is I; do not be afraid
set: After the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus has withdrawn to the mountain to avoid being made king (6:15). The disciples set out alone across the lake toward Capernaum. Mark 6:45–52 and Matthew 14:22–33 tell the same event; Matthew adds Peter’s walk on the water. John’s account is short and leads straight to the next day’s discourse.
str: vv. 16–18: evening, darkness, a rough sea, and Jesus absent.
vv. 19–20: Jesus comes over the water and speaks.
v. 21: they want to take him in, and at once they reach land.
kw: In John darkness is never only the time of day. “It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them” describes the disciples’ state as much as the hour (cf. 1:5).
The Greek says “twenty-five or thirty stades”, about five or six kilometres. The NRSV gives “three or four miles”. They are in the middle of the lake, far from either shore.
Literally “I am”. On the lips of Jesus in John these words often recall the divine name revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14), as in 8:58. Here they both identify him and reveal him.
vv: It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.
Many Christians know such nights: rowing hard with the Lord seemingly absent. John’s “not yet” promises that he is coming.
they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were terrified.
In the Old Testament it is God who “trampled the waves of the Sea” (Job 9:8). Jesus does what only God does.
It is I; do not be afraid.
The Lord’s first word is his presence, the second is peace. These are the words most often repeated in Scripture to frightened people.
immediately the boat reached the land toward which they were going.
Psalm 107 sings of sailors in a storm whom God brought “to their desired haven” (107:30). When Jesus is received, the journey reaches its end.
ch: From early times Christians have seen the boat as an image of the Church. Tertullian, writing on Baptism, says that the disciples’ little boat, tossed by the waves while the Lord slept, was a figure of the Church (in substance). The Church does not promise calm seas, but the presence of the Lord who comes over the waters and says, “It is I”.

study: Where in my parish or family is someone being overlooked, as the widows were? What could I do?
When has the Lord seemed absent while I was rowing in the dark? What helped me hear, “It is I”?
